To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the cross sections and velocity distributions for fragments with increased or decreased charge can be explained without invoking large energy or momentum losses, but that these fragments have large neutron losses that result in large proton excesses.

the cross section for production of charge-exchanged fragments with atomic numbers only changed by 1 to 3 is 0.1% of the interaction cross section; that the velocity of these fragments is determined primarily by the velocity of the incident nucleus; that the energy of these fragments is the same as that of the incident nuclei; and that the number of neutrons lost by these fragments, as well as by the fragments that lose a proton, is much larger than the number of protons lost.
the charge, mass, and kinetic energy changes during the breakup of relativistic nuclei are not large.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the fragmentation of nuclei is a complex process, but that the basic mechanism for the charge changes is the simple exchange of a proton with a target nucleus, with the exchange being accompanied by neutron loss.

the charge, mass, and kinetic-energy changes during the interaction of heavy nuclei with matter can be explained by the simple model of a charge exchange with a neutron pickup, without any significant energy loss in the process.

the charge and mass changes in the fragmentation of relativistically moving nuclei are very similar to those in the laboratory, except for the fact that, in the laboratory, there are many fewer fragments that have lost charge.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the charge, mass, and momentum changes in relativistic fragmentation are all well described by the simple picture that the projectile picks up or loses a proton or neutron, and that the momentum of these particles is transferred to the projectile.
the charge and energy changes that occur when a relativistic heavy nucleus fragments are not large.
the production of fragments by relativistic nuclei is a complex process, and the assumption that the charge of the incident nuclei is conserved during the fragmentation process is incorrect.
